utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Matthew Olmsted, Tom Hannis, and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, and Ms. Claire Plumb, appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic, Igor Pantelic, and Aleksandar Aleksic, appearing for Zupljanin Defence. Our client is not present. He already has signed a waiver.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I announced that I have two preliminary questions. One concerns the transcript of yesterday. I have an intervention. Page 16774, line 7, it is recorded as words of Mr. Krgovic, where in fact, it was myself who made the -- the submission. The second thing, Your Honours invited us to comment on the 17th motion for protective measures. Your Honours, we do oppose the motion. I will briefly explain. The first four witnesses which are referred to in the motion have been granted the protective measures in the previous cases based on the fact that they were viva voce witnesses. I am aware, and I know that -- that the protective measures applied in one cases proprio motu are adopted in the other cases. But, in my opinion, since these -- these witnesses are 92 bis witnesses, at least what our friends from the Office of the Prosecutor should have done was to approach the witnesses and ask them if they still insist on their protective measures based on the fact that they are 92 bis witnesses in this case. And we don't have any -- any information in that regard. The second group are two witnesses which are also 92 bis witnesses and are asking for protective measures for the first time. In both cases, we -- we lack the nature and the basis for -- for their concerns. The first one which returned to the -- to the territory of Republika Srpska and resides now in Doboj, we are inclined to -- to understand his concerns to a certain extent, but, still, nonetheless, I believe the witness should -- or the witness -- the Office of the Prosecutor should provide a certain additional information as the nature of these concerns. The second one which resides outside of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the moment, talks about his concerns based on some rally by the Serbs, asking to -- or asking to kill Croats and Muslims? I don't think that such a thing has -- has happened in -- in Bosnia and Herzegovina or Republika Srpska any time in last, at least, ten years. That is -- that is for sure, that such a rally happened and it wasn't made public or some measures were not taken, it's quite impossible. Therefore, based on that, that fact, I don't think that we can accept that as a truth. Perhaps the witness has some wrong information about it, because he doesn't reside, after all, in the territory. Those are the reasons why we oppose this motion. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you want to hear any response from us at this time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If are you in a position to, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm in a position --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, we do. When I say if you are in a position, if you are in a position to at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would make a brief submission at this time and then perhaps follow it up with something in writing if you need. With regard to the first four witnesses, they were granted protective measures in the previous case and the jurisprudence in the Tribunal is those apply in other cases mutatis mutandis, and there is a presumption that they apply. I know a case law that requires the Prosecution to go back to a witness and ask him, Do you still want those protective measures. And the fact that they are now 92 bis, the mode of testimony standing by itself does not seem to be, to me, a reason why you would change it. Generally, the reason that protective measures are sought by witnesses is because they fear if it is learned that they have given testimony in a case here or against particular accused, that they may suffer some consequences and if that testimony is presented live or 92 ter or 92 bis, either way the same concerns for the witness exist, whether they are seen in court live or whether somebody reads their statement or their transcript. They will know that that person has provided evidence and that's generally the causes for the witnesses having concerns about testifying here and being retaliated against, and that's why we speak protective measures. So for the first four, I don't think you have heard anything that would cause you to need to deviate from the norm of allowing those protective measures from previous cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We certainly accept that, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. With regard to the other two, I'm sorry, I'm not -- I'm not up to speed on their particular situations. I will review what Mr. Zecevic has said, speak with the lawyers dealing with those two witnesses, and get back to you as soon as I can. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. If there are no other preliminary matters, could the blinds be lowered so that the witness could be escorted back to the stand, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Witness. It has been reported to us that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That your health has improved over yesterday, and we trust that you're able to remain with us to complete your testimony today. I would only remind you, as I said yesterday, that if at any point that you are in distress, you could either indicate it to us or indicate it to the Court Officer and we will, of course, take a break in order to accommodate you. And, Mr. Olmsted, if you're ready, you may resume your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to begin by clarifying something that you testified about yesterday. Do you recall, I asked you that besides the buses that brought detainees to Omarska what other means were used to bring detainees to the camp. And you responded that they arrived by a vehicle known as an Marica. Do you remember testifying to that?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what kind of vehicle this was?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a blue vehicle, but there's one portion which is painted white. The majority of it is painted blue. But a smaller portion is white. It has protective bars on the windows.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And who used these vehicles?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: These vehicles were used by the police, and they belonged to the Prijedor SJB.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yesterday you testified that a police officer named Ranko Kovacevic typically brought detainees to Omarska camp. Would he use one of these vehicles when he was doing that?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot ascertain that it was he, himself, who used this vehicle, but he did on a number of occasions bring one, two, or three persons at any one time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: At the end of yesterday's session, we were talking about the 175 detainees who were -- remained behind at Omarska camp after the rest of the detainees were transferred to either Manjaca camp or Trnopolje camp. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have P668 on the screen. And this is tab 18. And if we could turn to page 2 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see this is a dispatch numbered 11-12-2169 from SJB Prijedor to CSB Banja Luka, dated 1 August 1992. If we look at the contents, we see that in this dispatch, Drljaca is informing the CSB that the War Presidency of the Prijedor Municipal Assembly adopted a decision to reduce the reserve police force and turn over the security of Keraterm, Trnopolje, and Omarska reception centres to the army. However, Drljaca writes that the army is refusing to accept responsibility, and, therefore, he was not in a position to implement the War Presidency's decision. Now, if we could take a look at 65 ter 505, which is tab 20, we see a dispatch from CSB Banja Luka to SJB Prijedor dated 4 August 1992, so just a few days later, and we see in the reference line that it references Drljaca's dispatch of 11-12-2169, the one we just looked at. Sir, in the upper right-hand corner we see in handwriting a list of names. Can you tell us who are these persons that are listed here?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Perhaps we can zoom in a little bit on the names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I know these names written here in pencil. The first one is Dusan Jankovic, then Marko Djenadija, then Milutin Cadjo, and the fourth one is Djuro Prpos.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us what positions they held at SJB Prijedor? You could skip the first one because I think we've already heard about him, but the other three, I think, are new.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which specific post Djenadija held. Milutin Cadjo was the police commander in Prijedor. And Djuro Prpos was the commander of the traffic police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So were all these persons in leadership positions at SJB Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could zoom out now to look at the contents of the dispatch.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see in this dispatch that the CSB chief agrees that SJB Prijedor may postpone the obligation of co-ordinating the number of reserve policemen pursuant to a CSB -- a prior CSB dispatch until adequate solutions are found together with the leadership of the army and in accordance with the War Presidency decisions. Sir, did the civilian police from Prijedor continue to provide security at Omarska until the very end of the camp?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we object to that. First of all, the one part of question is: Did witness ever see that and he has any knowledge about this dispatches and the contents of this dispatches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, there is a question -- I -- I don't know if -- well, I better ask the witness directly. Mr. Witness, what is the significance of these handwritten names to which Mr. Olmsted has referred you? It's a type written dispatch, and there is certain information written in manuscript and including the list of these names. What is the -- what are we to make of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, the practice was for the head of an organ, which, in this case, was Mr. Simo Drljaca. Once he receives a document, he writes the names of his assistants to be delivered or be given these dispatches for their information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it is a circulation list, or distribution list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to this, Djuro Prpos was supposed to assume responsibility for the task relating to the traffic. Milutin Cadjo as the commander should have taken responsibility for general police work. For Djenadija I said I don't know which duties he discharged and I know that Dusan Jankovic was Mr. Simo Drljaca's deputy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Olmsted, do you have a response to Mr. -- it seems to me the document is relevant, but do you have a response to Mr. Krgovic's objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, I don't think this is the first document that has been tendered through a witness who has not seen necessarily the document before, but he can speak to the contents with regard to staffing issues at least one of the camps, Omarska, and he has also been able now to identify some of the people on the distribution list. This relates to a document that has already been admitted into evidence. We -- see that there is a reference number in the heading, 11-12-2169, which is to the previous document. So it is relevant, it is probative, and this witness has been able to provide some evidence with regard to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't see anywhere in this document any mention of security of Omarska or any other centres. This document purely relates to the reduction of the number of reserve police officers. The Prosecutor avoided to ask the witness anything about this specific item. Quite the contrary, he paraphrased the document and quoted from the document something which is not written in it. If you look at the contents carefully, it has nothing to do with the security of the centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, those arguments go to the weight. And, of course, they can be reserved for the end of this case. Obviously, the Defence and the Prosecution have different positions with regard to this document. But the question here is whether it can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber rules that the document may be admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document shall assigned Exhibit P1682. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, I now want to show you a video of -- that perhaps -- from 1992 that perhaps you can help us identify some individuals on it. Before I do, do you recall a group of internationals coming to Omarska in early August 1992?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we have 65 ter 1444 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This, as we can see from the bottom, is an order from Lieutenant-General Ratko Mladic from VRS Main Staff dated 3 August 1992. If we look at item number 1, Mladic orders that the army immediately undertake measures through the MUP authorities to arrange POW camps in your zones of responsibility and prepare them for the visits by foreign journalists and International Red Cross team. If we look just briefly under items 2 and 3, we see that Mladic indicates that the plan is for the internationals to visit Omarska, Trnopolje and Manjaca in the zone of the 1st Krajina Corps responsibility. Sir, can you tell us what preparations did the police at Omarska undertake before the internationals arrived at the camp?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one day before we received information that representatives of the International Red Cross would be coming to visit the camp. For that purpose, certain measures were undertaken in order to put this area, in order where the individuals who stayed in Omarska were kept, in terms of cleaning the space. We brought in additional beds. And that would be more or less what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, may this be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P1683. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I would now like to bring up the video. This is P1357. Tabs 16 in our binder. We're not going to play the sound. This has already been played for the Trial Chamber through a prior witness and I'm not really interested in what is said during this footage. I'm more interested in the witness helping us identify certain locations and persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: May we just go back a few seconds. Maybe just start it from the very beginning. Yes. There we go. We paused it at 13 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this location, where these vehicles are approaching?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That should be one section of the Omarska mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And let's move to 18 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We saw a gate there. And yesterday you were telling us about a first- and second-ring of security that surrounded Omarska camp. Would this be the gate to enter the first ring or the second ring?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the first ring.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now we see an individual coming out from what looks like a booth at the gate. Can you tell us what kind of shirt he's wearing?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he is wearing some kind of blue shirt. A shade of blue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Maybe we can just play a little bit of -- so maybe can get a closer look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was this a shirt that was worn by any members of any organisation at the time?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the policemen wore blue shirts, but they had epaulettes and he should have had some insignia on them. However, I don't see any such thing on this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's play a little bit further.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I want to pause at 40 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recognise this person?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Who he is?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is Mladen Radic, a police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recall what position he held at the Omarska camp?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a policeman, but I heard from other people - he didn't tell that to me personally - that he was a shift leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's continue forward and pause at 47 second.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: This man that's in this image here, it appears that he has some kind of wound on his face. And my question to you is: Did the police guards bring detainees with fresh bruises or cuts on their face to the interrogation rooms for interrogation? Were there instances of that?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I personally saw only one such case of Becir Medunjanin but he was brought in with other individuals from Kosara where the army was mopping up the terrain and they were found hiding in that area. As for the others, I personally didn't see them but I do not rule out the possibility that there were individual cases of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when you say Becir Medunjanin, can you describe what you saw on him, what injuries he had?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he had bruises and hematoma on the face, and he had a piece of gauze in his nostril.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's go forward to 50 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see now a man who appears to be emaciated. Did the police guards bring detainees in this kind of physical condition to the interrogation rooms?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that, because people were fully dressed; whereas, this person here is only in his undershirt.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's move forward to 1 minute and 3 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sorry, let's move back to -- I'll say when we pause. Yes, that's fine, right there. At 1 minute and 2 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you tell us what kind of uniform this person with the rifle is wearing?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He has an epaulette on the shoulder with some insignia, but I cannot discern the colour. It might have been the jacket that he is wearing, because there were not enough uniforms, so I cannot recognise the colour. I can only see that he has some insignia on the shoulder which should indicate that he was a policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: What colour were the reserve policemen's uniforms during this time-period?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no uniform pattern because there was shortage of uniforms. A number of reserve police officers had incomplete uniforms. They either had a shirt or the trousers; whereas, the active-duty policemen had full uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's move -- fast-forward to 1 minute and 40 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We can pause, yes, there, 1 minute and 40 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see two individuals here. Do you know these persons?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This gentleman is Simo Drljaca. I don't know the other person, but I know that she worked as a translator for journalists and for the people from the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Do you recognise this office?

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Yes, I can -- well, I thought I saw Judge Harhoff reaching forward. That probably should be redacted that last answer. I didn't anticipate that he would provide that information in that detail. And may we just go briefly into private session, so I can ask a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we can move forward -- I think we can just fast-forward to 2 minutes and 29 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see three men in camouflage. The one in the middle is wearing a blue beret. Can you tell us who that person is?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Mr. Zeljko Mejakic, the commander of the security in the Omarska camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: We see a man in a blue camouflage uniform. Do you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is, although I don't see his face fully, but I think it is Vokic, Radovan, who was a driver and he also an escort for Mr. Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And we see a man in a camouflage uniform to the right of Mr. Mejakic. Who is that person?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's Mr. Simo Drljaca, and the other person in the camouflage uniform, I don't see him that well, and I really cannot identify him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let's just move forward a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now we see that third individual in the camouflage uniform. Can you -- do you know who he is?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an a military officer, but I don't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I suggest we go in a private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So in the big cafeteria at Keraterm, because there was a shortage of offices, interviews were conducted simultaneously in four different corners with four different individuals. Statements were being taken from them. And for each of the interviews, there would be two operatives; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it went on for about one or two days, because we stayed there for two days only.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think this had to be redacted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please go on, sir. Do try and not mention the names who were there with you. You are a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had an office that was on first floor, and there were three of us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: During your time in the Keraterm building during the interviews, did you go from office to office? Did you enter the cafeteria where interviews of several individuals were conducted simultaneously?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I had enough time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Have you noticed any incidents of physical abuse, of mistreating by investigators against people interviewed?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not during the two days that we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After the two or maybe three days, you again faced the problem of insufficient space, bearing in mind the number of people that were to be interviewed.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's just my assumption. I did not make such a decision. I don't know what the reason was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, it is a fact that on the last day of May, or about that date, you moved to the offices and the buildings of the Omarska mine.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You're aware that on the 30th of May an attack occurred, an armed attack, against the town of Prijedor during which several people were killed.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The attack was carried out by Muslim units; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Primarily Muslim, but there were also individuals who were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see Mr. Olmsted stood up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Again, I'm going raise the same objection. I did not lead any evidence on any attack on Prijedor. Just regarding -- I just led evidence on what was occurring at Omarska camp itself. All this evidence -- we don't know where he is getting this information from, whether it's first-hand knowledge, whether it's from the interrogations conducted at the facilities. But my main objection, of course, is, you know, where is the adjudicated fact that this particularly goes to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, again this is -- this is simply context. I would appreciate if Mr. Olmsted be reminded that he is not supposed to laugh while I'm talking. Thank you very much. This was the second time. First time I didn't intervene. This is the second time and I don't think that is appropriate behaviour for a counsel in the courtroom. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I understood your explanation about context in terms of the first intervention but could you assist me with this one? I -- this seems to be completely outside --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's the same reason, Your Honours. They are moving from the SJB building because it was inadequate for the number of people. They're moving to Keraterm. Now, in the meantime when they are in Keraterm, there has been attack on Prijedor, and another number of people has been arrested during that -- or post that attack. Because of that, again, for the purposes of inadequacy, they are moved from Keraterm to Omarska to investigation centre or the Omarska mine. That is precisely the context I want to explore with the witness, nothing more, nothing less. But I'm perfectly willing to ask the witness whether he has first-hand information about these attacks or -- specifically about this attack on Prijedor on the 30th of May. But I didn't thought that that was -- that was a contested issue, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I don't want to such a question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Hold on. Exactly, Mr. Zecevic, since this is not contested, I think it is clear and I fully understand the point where you are going, but the fact that they moved from Keraterm to Omarska, the witness has already explained it, and the reasons why they moved is clear already in the witness's testimony. So I'm just wondering if you have any specific need to repeat this evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, with all due respect, it was one question: Is he aware of the attack on Prijedor on the 30th of May? That is the only question I wanted to ask. Mr. Olmsted objected, and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, from the moment when you moved to Omarska, and I should say that you stayed there from the very beginning until the very end; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think that yesterday you said that -- but please, if you're not feeling well, do tell us and we'll take a break. I don't want to put any pressure on you.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's all right. You can continue for a period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ten minutes would be all right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think that yesterday you said that you and the teams of inspectors who conducted the interviews worked at Omarska from the morning until late in the evening; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the case for a number of days. However, our standard working time was from 8.00 until 4.00 p.m. But since over the period of some days, large number of individuals were brought in, the chief, Simo Drljaca, ordered us to work until 8.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, your evidence on page 16750 of yesterday, I believe that you said that eight investigating teams conducted concurrently interviews with certain individuals.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, my learned friend showed you document P1560. That's a decision on the setting up an investigation centre signed by Mr. Simo Drljaca and the centre was to be established in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can we please have P1650.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You remember it?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to page 2, item 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to ask you this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in English that should be page three, and page 2 in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you see here that under item 13, the chief of the public security station emphasises that all the authorised officials in -- at this collection centre "shall observe the positive legislation and rules of service. In particular, they must keep official secrets ..."

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since you said that you hadn't seen this document before yesterday, let me ask you this: Were you aware of what is stated under item 15, which is on page 3 in the Serbian, that the chief of the public security station strictly forbade divulging any information without his approval. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you acted in compliance with that. We heard that both you and your colleague who was in charge of the inspectors from the public security went to the SJB every morning, in order to submit daily reports to the chief of the SJB, the late Mr. Simo Drljaca.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I know that the witness said that he was able to cope, but, judging by his facial impressions, I think that this would be a good time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you -- thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We would rise for a half-hour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I discussed with the Registrar, and I just wanted to inform, and ask the permission of the Trial Chamber, because of the condition of the witness, we were told that the doctor suggests that his back is at the 90 degrees and therefore he has a problem when -- when he is moving over to see the documents on the screen. So I propose that I -- that we print out all the documents that I intend to show him so he can have a file in front of him, in order that he be able to -- to -- to check the contents of the documents while sitting normally and doesn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If that's more convenient. Certainly, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And also, if he wants to stand up every once in a while, he can just do that. Please tell him so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, would Your Honours give him that instruction or shall I instruct him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, there is something else I am about to inform. So I could tell him at the same time. Mr. Witness, we have determined that we will take a break after ever 60 minutes rather that going to the usual 80 minutes and counsel has indicated that to minimise the necessity for you to lean over to see the screen, they're going provide you with paper copies of documents. But in addition to that, if it is more convenient for you to stand rather than sit at any point during your testimony, please feel you are at liberty to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday, at page 16751 of your testimony, you said that initially, if I understood your evidence correctly, you divided or categorised people that you interviewed based on the place that they hailed from. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And, again, if I understood you correctly, you divided them into people who came from Gornja Puharska, from Donja Puharska, from Hambarine, from Kozarac; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, how long was this categorisation in place? A week, ten days?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until we concluded preliminary interviews with everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And when you concluded preliminary interviews, then you categorised them into three categories; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it was possible to transfer somebody from the second category into the first category, if we received good information about his negative activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify, so you would conduct a preliminary interview with a person, and the person would deny that he participated in an armed rebellion, for example, following which you would categorise him as the second category. However, following him, a next interviewee would come along and confirm that the previous person was, for example, a company commander, indicating that the first person lied, based on which you would transfer that person from category 2 into category 1. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I suppose that the three categories that we discussed, that that system was formulated some time in late June, roughly; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in your testimony, you said that about 3.000 or 3.100 persons went through the Omarska investigation centre and that all of them were interviewed; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Except that a small number of people was interviewed twice. Precisely for the reasons you mentioned earlier. Because the witnesses were not frank. I apologise, not witnesses, but interviewees.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You confirmed to us that the first category in that system of categorisation that you had was housed in that white house on the side, that some of them were housed there, and also, in the hangars in the garages that were located under the offices where you conducted interviews; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the photograph 65 ter 2234. You saw this photograph yesterday. Remember that?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you marked this photograph.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To the extent that I was able to understand this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, please, if we could mark something that wasn't marked yesterday. I hope this will not present a huge problem for you. Could we ask for the assistance of the usher to help you mark the white house. Could you mark the white house by number 1. Just a moment, please. They need to prepare everything before you mark it. Just a moment, please. The Court Usher will prepare the screen for you. Please mark the white house by placing number 1 next to it.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Also, the garages where your offices were on the left. Could you mark it by placing number 2.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now tell me, please, the building in front of the building where your offices were, where you conducted preliminary interviews, I suppose that that is the dining-room.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you put number 3 next to it.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, when asked by His Honour Judge Delvoie, you explained that some of the persons from the second and third category stayed in the large building which, on the ground floor, had the garages for the large mining trucks. The persons used the -- the persons were in the offices that had previously been used by the workers on the first floor of the building; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you mark it by placing number 4.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And if there are no objections, I would tender this into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit 1D393. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, can I just put one follow-up question on this photograph with the markings. Mr. Witness, the building you marked with number 2, I understand you did your work on the offices on the first floor. And I hear now that on the second floor -- on the ground floor of that particular building there were garages; is that right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the one side, yes, there were garages. Under the floor where we worked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in the premises that were located under the offices where you conducted preliminary interviews, this is where the people from the first category stayed; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that's how it was, although it was the security commander who was in charge of that. He and his people were supposed to allocate premises where people would be placed, but I think that you were -- you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown P5670. That is the document you saw yesterday and I have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a letter - I don't know if you remember it - this letter by Simo Drljaca dated the 5th of August, 1992, where, in the second paragraph, it says that the -- by way of investigation it was established that 1.466 people are criminally liable and there is valid documentation to support it and that they will be transferred under guard to the Manjaca military camp on the 6th of August, 1992? Do you remember that these people were transferred to the Manjaca camp some time in early August?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, please look at the document.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for providing the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Have you looked at the document?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested is something to which you already replied. Tell me, please, if I understood your evidence well, after these people were taken to Manjaca, the people belonging to categories 1 and 2, and the people in category 3 were transferred to Trnopolje, some 175 persons remained also from category 1. They were the ones who remained at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. I mean Omarska.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And these people were also subsequently transferred to Manjaca in late August 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, if my calculations are correct, given that 3.000 or 3.100 persons went through the Omarska investigation centre, that means, if we accept that they were transferred to Manjaca on the 6th of August, to Manjaca, Trnopolje, that means that within some 65 working days, you interviewed all 3.100 individuals. You conducted preliminary interviews with 3.100 individuals; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we worked sometime until the 3rd of August doing these preliminary interviews and then organising the documentation. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So maybe even less, some 62 or 63 days, and some people were interviewed more than once; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If my calculations are right, that would mean that you interviewed over 50 persons per day.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's quite possible. We had ten teams. Some interviews were shorter. We didn't take long with some individuals because they did not present -- they were not -- they did not have any relevant security information to provide. And sometimes we worked until 10.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the need to conduct preliminary interviews with these individuals was based on the intelligence that those individuals had been involved in commission of some crimes; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what the rules of service of police set forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When I say "crimes," I'm referring to preparations for armed rebellion, murder, causing public danger, unlawful possession of weapons and the like.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So these people were interviewed because, in accordance with the laws in force at the time, there were grounds to believe that they had committed a crime; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the persons you interviewed were not interviewed only because they were Muslims or because they were of Muslim faith.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not solely because of that. It was mostly because of their criminal activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You told me earlier, that in relation to each individual, there were grounds to believe that they were involved in some crimes, that there was intelligence indicating that.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But through further investigation and through intelligence gathered afterwards, it was established that that could not be proven in relation to some individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: However, sir, before you conducted these preliminary interviews, you couldn't have known whether this intelligence would be subsequently confirmed or denied. It was only after an interview that you could assess whether there were, indeed, reasonable grounds to suspect somebody or there were no elements to suspect them of having been involved in some crimes.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said yesterday in my evidence that our position, the position of our group which conducted that work, was that documents need to be provided supporting these reasonable grounds in relation to these individuals. However, documents did not arrive in relation to each individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And this is why you had to conduct preliminary interviews with these persons in order to establish whether there were, indeed, reasonable grounds to prosecute them or not.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did that, and we categorised them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is a fact, isn't it, that while conducting preliminary interviews and while assessing the outcome of these preliminary interviews, you established that some of these individuals were clearly involved in armed rebellion; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that the individuals in questions [as interpreted] were organised into some military or quasi-military structures.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: They had their commanding officers, lower-rank officers, and the entire command structure; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: These individuals were involved in carrying out combat operation, armed attacks.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some them, some groups were involved in the attack against Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: They were captured during military operations.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many of individuals from that category were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, we've seen in the previous document, or, rather, on the photograph, that you were located in the offices within the building you marked with number 2. In -- if you feel the need to stand up ...

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's okay. I'm fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If at any point you feel the need to do something -- you've been told also by the Trial Chamber that you shouldn't hesitate to say so.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not a problem. Thank you. You can carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the offices were on the first floor of the building you marked with number 2. In the same building, as you told us, there were eight to ten investigation teams doing preliminary interviews. Most of the offices were on the first floor, with the exception of two offices that were on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And, according to your testimony yesterday, when you talked about an incident during which you heard wailing of someone from a different room, adjoining room, you entered that room and saw the individual on the floor and then concluded there was physical abuse and mistreatment of this individual behind that.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the fact is that, if I understood you well, that on that floor you could hear and in each such incident, of course, if there were any, you could also hear how the interviews were being conducted, whether there was any physical abuse or mistreatment of the individuals; am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one could hear but not from all the offices, because this office was next to ours. And talking about the physical abuse, through conversations between us, we have gathered that these would take place after we'd left, in the afternoon hours, for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In other words, during the time when you were conducting interviews, such instances, such incidents were very rare. You talk about this one case, but these people were not physically abused during the time while you were there.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would have short meetings during the working day in the hall, first the two -- three of us then the two of us, during which we would inform our inspectors that they should act according to what they're authorised to do, after which they would go and conduct the interviews. I mentioned this case because the office in question was adjacent to the one where we were; whereas, the other offices were lined up along the building from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But if I understood you correctly, you told us now that you, although held those briefings every day, that you advised your inspectors that they should act properly and comply with the authorisation that they had, and that incidents like the one you have described to us, where physical abuse took place during the interview, that such instances were rather rare?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know only of that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You did confirm that such incidents were rare and that you do not know of other such incidents?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You told us a moment ago that the physical abuse would take place during the afternoon hours, after your departure from the investigation centre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I want go back to the previous question and your conclusion you did confirm -- well, firstly the witness answered to one of your question, "Well, I know only of that case." And then you say, "You did confirm that such incidents were rare ..." Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- a statement he made somewhere else or is that something you conclude from his previous answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, my question to the witness was, "And that incidents like that," this is page 40, line 5: "Incidents like that, the one you had described to us where physical abuse took place during the interview, that such instances were rather rare?" And the witness answered yes: "I know only of that one case."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well the transcript --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't recorded properly and that is why I asked another question to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So you say the answer was yes, I know only of this case. And not, well, I only know of this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. He said yes, I know only of this case and that is why I returned again to the question again and he confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, just for the transcript, you answered in affirmative to my question. You told us that there was just one such incident that you knew of?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, sir -- just a moment, please. Was this mistreatment that took place in the afternoon hours after your departure from the investigation centre, was that in any way related to the content or requirements related to the preliminary interviews?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot claim that that prompted it, but it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is why I'm asking you this. For instance, in the morning, you interview one or several individuals, individuals who, during the interview, say they were not involved in any armed rebellion. And after your departure in the afternoon, somebody physically mistreats that person, would that be because the person who physically mistreated an individual was caused by the fact that this person had said something or had not said something during the interview? Can you confirm this in any way?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is possible, but I -- I cannot confirm that for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In any case, as far as you were concerned, and your inspectors, the operatives, the abuse that may have taken place in the afternoon was not something that had been initiated by you or your people.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I can say that it wasn't. I believe that it wasn't done by my inspectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You did talk about one case where not only physical abuse but elimination of 18 persons was initiated by a state -- public security inspector. You told us about it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: During the preliminary interviews, could you tell us what kind of methodology was applied? Would the person be interviewed and then asked to write a statement; or was the statement based on the notes taken by the inspectors during the interview?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The inspectors would be drafting Official Notes. We would go through them, and once we would assess that an Official Note was of security interest, we would then draft a statement based on it, and the inspector who conducted the interview would sign the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So the inspectors would conduct a preliminary interview with an individual and would take notes, Official Notes during the interview. After the interview would be finished, they would release the person and bring the Official Notes to you for you to make an assessment whether there's anything of security interest in the Official Note; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And upon determining there is information of security interest or intelligence in a note, then a statement would be typed. Let's go step by step. First, the statement would be typed; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And then the individual would be brought in to sign the statement. The authorised officer would also sign the statement and that would be it. There were cases, though, where some people would not be completely frank, and then we would repeat the interview and either make an addendum to the original statement or take a new statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, I just need an information. When do we need to break, because I'm a bit confused? I don't remember when we started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was thinking it would be noon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ten minutes before ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We would break at 11.50 until 12.10.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, with the help of the usher, I'd like to hand a document over to you. It would make it easier for you to go through these printed versions, hard copies. I'll show you some documents that we have, some Official Notes that we have in our files, and I would like to ask you to confirm whether these are Official Notes taken in the Omarska investigation centre. As you can see, on the right-hand side, there are the blue tabs, and I'll identify documents using the tabs. I'll first ask for the document to be put on the screen and then tell you where it is in this folder. The first document I want to show to you is 1D00-3275, which is tab 33.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We have to wait for it to appear on the screen. This is a list including 195 individuals. We cannot tell who is the author of this document. There are no indications with the exception of the title saying: "Aggressors on Prijedor." I assume it -- what's meant by it is the people who took part in the attack on Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As can you see here, the names Slavko Ecimovic, Mehmed Okic and so on, do you recognise these names as names of individuals who had been interviewed in investigation centre Omarska?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about some of them, yes. Under 1, it is Ecimovic, Slavko, who was a leader of one group that was involved in the attack against Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you this --

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kemal Alagic led another group on the attack in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You mean number 24, Kemal Alagic?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, one question: Is it your recollection that some 200 persons participated in the attack on Prijedor and that you conducted preliminary interviews with them?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to our information, four groups took part in the attack on Prijedor. They had the task to capture vital facilities in Prijedor municipality. Through our investigation, we learned that one group was supposed to take the Municipal Assembly group -- building. The other group was supposed to take "Kozarski Vjesnik" newspaper building and take over all the media. The third group was supposed to take up the railway station to take up positions there. And as for the fourth group, I can't remember. No, they were supposed to capture the post office, the PTT and telecom building.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, these four groups, how strong were they roughly?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact number, but whether it's the number that you mentioned, I can't confirm that. But those were large groups and an armed conflict erupted where a large number of MUP staff was killed and a number of civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "a number of civilians," are you referring to the residents of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that Bosko Zujic was killed on that occasion. The driver of the ambulance was wounded, Dragojevic. He was gravely wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have a suggestion, during the break, which should be quite soon, could you take the documents binder with you and go over the documents so that we can save time. So if you could go over the names and see which names you recognise and can provide additional information and let's proceed that way. And, in the meantime, I'll put another question to you. We saw a bit earlier the letter of the 5th of August. I think that's P670, where Mr. Drljaca says that it has been established that 1.466 persons, that there are reasonable grounds to believe that they committed crimes that are punishable under the law; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the data from the SJB. But I think that that included also persons who were outside of the Omarska investigation centre. Because the police conducted their work throughout the municipality, and I can't say that it was precisely that number of people related to the Omarska investigation centre. I think that that data applied to the entire territory of the municipality, to the entire territory under the jurisdiction of that SJB.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us, roughly, how many people there were? We heard how many people went through interviews at Omarska investigation centre. It was 3.100 persons. Out of that number, based on your recollections, for how many of them it was confirmed that there were reasonable grounds to believe they had committed crimes?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, those were mostly people from the first category, and there were other 1.000 of them. The first and second category.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, 47, line 2, I think you said from the first and second category, which was over 1.000 persons; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The transcript reflected only the first category, and that's why I asked you. You told us that some people were prosecuted or proceedings were instituted against them by military organs; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will read out some names for you. Sead Cirkin. Do you remember that that person was prosecuted by the military judicial organs?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Muhic, Asim.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of a person from the military with the last name of Muhic but I'm not sure it's the same person. Based on our investigation, we were able to establish that that Muhic took part in the attack on Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Kemal Alagic. Do you know that he also was prosecuted by the military judiciary.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible because the army arrested him when clearing up the terrain, after the attack on Prijedor, sometime after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's a good time to have a break so that the witness could go over these documents and that would significantly shorten the time needed for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well. So we would return in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Lower the blinds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, you may escort the witness from the courtroom. We're just waiting ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can we continue, sir?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I have a few questions for you. First of all, you have had years of experience as an operative in the service of the State Security Service; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You explained to us what methodology was applied in the course of the interviews that were conducted within the Omarska investigation centre.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So once you've been through the Official Notes drafted by the inspectors and after the statement would be drafted, a statement that was signed by the interviewee and the authorised official, this signature by the interviewed individual was there to confirm the accuracy of the contents of the statement.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: While you were going through the Official Notes before drafting the statement, you would, on occasion, bring the individual in to give an additional statement.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In fact, you would cross-reference information received from several individuals, verify them, and try to determine the truth, based on that work.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After a statement regarding an individual was drafted, the individual would be presented with the statement and asked to sign it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The individuals who were signing the statements, were they being forced to sign or whether they did it on a voluntary basis?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, they were not forced to sign the statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So, according to your information, they were not forced to sign the relevant statements.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind that you cross-referenced, verified the information, the facts that would be contained in a statement would be something that would have a confirmation in the fact -- facts that could be found in statements by other people interviewed.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In other words, according to you, there were no reason to doubt the truth of the statements.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In regard to those statements that were taken in my presence or where I was involved, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, in the office we had seen in video footage recently, you analysed all the Official Notes and documentation you'd get from the inspectors.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And on the basis of the notes, you cross-referenced the information, verified it, and then drafted the statements.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And that applied to all the statements taken during your time in Omarska investigation centre.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "mostly," that was precisely what I referred to as well. In your view, all the statements, there is no reason to doubt the accuracy, the truthfulness of the statements; am I right there?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, did you have time to go through the binder I gave you?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Have you found any Official Notes or statements you can recognise as those taken in the Omarska investigation centre?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let's deal with that. 1D04-3379, tab 10 in our binder. This is an Official Note made on the basis of interview with Mehmed Jakupovic drafted on the 29th of May, 1992. I assume that this note could not have been drafted in the Omarska investigation centre because of the date, 29th of May. That was from before establishment of Omarska as an investigation centre but it should have been taken in Keraterm. Can you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the -- a format that we used for such Official Notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So there is the format of Official Notes.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask to you take a look at page 2 of this document, where we can see the initials of the authorised officer.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you recognise whose initial this is?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you with any certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What we see here is that there is no signature by the interviewee, Mr. Mehmed Jakupovic. However, it is a fact, isn't it, that the Official Notes were drafted and then several copies would be made of them?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Official Notes were typed in, yes, several copies, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In how many copies; can you remember?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in two copies. It all depended on whether they would be also submitted to some other organisational units. One would go to the archives that were kept within the public security station; and the other copy would stay with the inspector, the operative, who ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And the individual with whom the interview was carried would sign just one copy. The other copy would be the one for the archives; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information that would be transferred from an Official Note -- actually, each page of the statement would get an initial. The statement would contain information from Official Notes and then it would be signed, and only such signed version would be legally valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In any case, can you recognise this Official Note as an example of the format of Official Notes taken at that time, either in SJB Prijedor or Keraterm, for the three days, and, later on, in Omarska.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a standard format for Official Notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know this person, Mehmed Jakupovic?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know him personally but there was a hamlet in Kozarac area where many people had that surname. From the note you can see that there are many people with the same surname.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this document was sent for translation and I would like to tendered it and MFI it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would ask for a clarification. Is this document being tendered just to show as an example of the procedure that was followed for taking Official Notes or written statements by persons in the custody of the SJB? If that's the case, then I'm not sure if it is even necessary to admit because I don't think there is any contention between the parties that Official Notes or official statements were taken from various detainees. If it is being sought to be admitted for the truth of its contents, I do have a strong objection to that, and -- but I will first seek a clarification from Mr. Zecevic on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we are talking here about the knowledge of this witness on taking the Official Notes and the statements of the interviews during the time that he performed that in SJB Prijedor, Keraterm, and Omarska investigation centres. I offer these documents for two purposes: For the purpose of showing the form, how it was; and for the truth of its contents. Absolutely, yes. The witness confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Then, Your Honours, I would ask that the witness remove his headsets so that we can have some argument on this particular issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Could the witness remove his head phones. Mr. Zecevic, it seems to me that, as Mr. Olmsted has said in terms of showing what happened in terms of method that we already need the -- this is an exhibit, but I'm curious as to the basis on which you would be seek to be tendering this for the truth of its contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, the witness confirmed that a certain procedure was followed in accordance with the rules of the -- of -- of -- the rules that guide the police according to the law in -- in the process of getting the official statements and the statements by the people who are interviewed during these interviews. I think I sufficiently established the opinion of this witness that most of the -- of the statements taken, which he saw, were cross-referenced, were analysed, were created, and then they were signed without any pressure, which means voluntary. And that he, himself, doesn't have a doubt about the truth of its contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I might interrupt you there. That last point is really irrelevant, isn't it, the witness's opinion as to a particular item of potential evidence. So that would strike me as being the weakest plank in your platform.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, he is the officer that took the statements. If he says the statements were given voluntarily that the statements were cross-referenced, analysed, and checked and were confirmed by other statements of other interviewees, I -- I don't think that that I can move anywhere further in that -- in that -- in that respect, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Zecevic, since the Chamber is unable to immediately appreciate the contents, my question is: What is this document, really?
