Is that one of the statements that was signed by a detainee after being interrogated, or is it -- what is it? I can see some names and the word pistol. So is that a list of weapons found with certain persons or ... what is it? Can you clarify it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand the problem because -- but unfortunately, we do not have translation for this particular document. This is the Official Note of -- of the -- of the talks with one Jakupovic, Mehmed, in which this person explains what happened in the village of Kevljani in the wider area of Kozarac, and who of the -- of the persons had what kind of a weapon. And it refers to Kevljani and the village of Poljaci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But, Mr. Zecevic, this would be a number of -- we know from the testimony of this witness about interviews being conducted. Indeed, the bringing up a particular document doesn't, to my mind, advance the strength of his testimony in terms of the procedure. And it must follow logically that a part of this process is that some analysis would be done. What I am completely at a loss to appreciate is why you would seek to tender this particular document, because it doesn't advance us any way beyond what we already know from what -- from the witness's testimony or what can reasonably be inferred from the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I must say, I do agree with Your Honour. This -- this particular document does not. But there has been a number of occasions during this trial when we wanted to introduce the statements of the witnesses who testified before Your Honours for -- in -- in -- given to the officials of the -- of the MUP in 1992 or in 1991. In each and every situation, the -- the objection was raised by -- by our friends from the Office of the Prosecution as allegedly these statements were taken under duress. And for these reasons, these statements were not accepted. Now, we have a situation here that, among these -- some of these documents, we will have the statements of the witnesses who hadn't appeared before this Trial Chamber but will appear in the future. And that is why I think, or -- or -- at the very least, there a motion pending to include those witnesses to the OTP case. That is why I -- I'm using this opportunity to introduce some of these statements, if the Court allows me to do that, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, is this of a witness who - to use your words - will appear?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge, Your Honour. But it might be relevant because I don't know what the witness will say. He might be able to give some evidence about these two villages, and then this statement might turn out to be relevant, or this Official Note. I'm just doing this out of the caution, no other reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I don't know if Your Honours want to hear from me. It was my original objection, but ... I think Your Honours are on the same wave length as I am, as far as the problems with this. This witness does not remember this person being a detainee at Omarska, does not remember this individual. This is it an unsigned statement. The witness has testified that he can only vouch for the Official Notes that he, himself, was present when the person signed them as to whether those statements were signed voluntarily or not. And we don't know how many of those and we certainty don't know that this particular one was presented to this witness. Mr. Zecevic is trying to get around Rule 92 bis. This person, Mehmed Jakupovic, has testified before this Tribunal. What he is essentially doing is opening the door for us to call Mr. Jakupovic in order to testify as to whether this particular statement was voluntary or not, and we don't want to go down that route at this stage on these proceedings. But that's the way we would have to go because really that is what is required, is to hear from the person who actually gave the statement as to whether it was voluntary, whether it was truthful, as he will have that direct knowledge of that. There is evidence that's already been presented, that's already here, there's adjudicated facts as to what was happening in Omarska during this time-period. So even if this witness was in Omarska and gave this statement in Omarska, it is going to be highly suspect and open to questions of reliability given the circumstances in which that statement was given. And so our position -- and I also have to note that this is a sampling -- these are the ones that the Defence want to use as part of their case, but they're probably a large number of these statements that would show the opposite, that would disprove the information contained in this particular statement. And are we going to open the door for the Prosecution now to go through, say, a thousand statements and pick out the ones that it believes supports what actually happened in Prijedor in April and May of 1992. So we object to the admission of this document or any others that the Defence intends to show this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I'm sorry, I still have not quite understood what this document really is. Can you clarify whether the person mentioned at the end of the document, Mr. Jakupovic, was he a detainee or was he someone who conducted an investigation about the weapons found in that village?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would love to be able to give that you information, Your Honour. However, I don't -- I don't know whether he was a detainee. I just have this -- this is the official recording of his interview. And I wasn't aware that the person has testified before this -- this Tribunal at all. It is probably from some of the other cases, which were not disclosed to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But, still, my question is: Was Mr. Jakupovic the guy who took the interview from someone else; or was he the guy who was being interviewed and gave this information?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. Mr. Jakupovic was the interviewee, so the one who gave the interview to the -- it says here the authorised official person. On the second page, there is some kind of a signature of the authorised official person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The decision of the Trial Chamber is that the document should not be marked for identification because, in terms of the contents, until it is interpreted, it isn't clear as to what -- it isn't clear -- apparent to the Trial Chamber as exactly what it seeks to convey. And in terms of the method and system to which it speaks, the testimony of the witness sufficiently establishes that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I understand. In that case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Sorry. I should have indicated when we started that, balancing the need to maximise as much time for today as possible with the needs of the witness, what we would do is break at 1.00 and then resume at 1.15 and then sit for an additional half-hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. Your Honour, I have one of the documents -- well, a couple of them, actually that have the translation. Maybe -- maybe that will help the Trial Chamber. I'm not trying to revisit the -- the issue. I know what is the ruling of the Trial Chamber but I just wanted to show this -- another document to the witness, and in order that the Trial Chamber will have a full appreciation of the document maybe, if I may proceed [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I see Mr. Hannis on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, if I may make an intervention now. I don't know if it will save time later on or not. But if Mr. Zecevic is going to attempt to introduce a written statement of a detainee at Omarska that was taken in 1992, we have an objection to all of those. We see this as a attempt to subvert the provision of Rule 92. He is trying to introduce a document for its contents, for the truth of its contents, of a witness who is not present. And that written statement doesn't conform with the requirements of the Rule of how they are supposed to be taken. In addition, we have an adjudicated fact in this case already. I think it is Fact 347, which says prisoners, after their interrogation, were often made to sign false statements regarding their involvement in acts versus Serbs. So unless he can ask this witness about a specific statement of a specific person that this witness was present for, we object to any attempt to introduce any of those other went written statements. If he wants to call some of those witnesses in the Defence case, say, Yes, that's my statement and I made it and it was true and it was not under duress, then he can do it then. But otherwise, you should not permit this to go forward. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It seems to me, Mr. Zecevic, that Mr. Hannis has succinctly and accurately stated the position in this matter about the -- I don't -- the particular document that you had indicated you are moving on to, how is that different from the last one? And how is it -- how -- how is it different from the point that Mr. Hannis has just addressed?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we definitely challenge the Fact 347. We say -- we say that that these statements were accurate, were not false statements and were not given under duress or anything like that. And that is what the witness basically testified to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yeah. Fair enough. But is the statement that you're about to move to, as I understand it, one that this witness would have taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, with all due respect, we -- the witness denied the -- his willingness to meet with the Defence. So this is the Office of the Prosecutor's witness. I gave him the binder. The only thing I can do is ask the witness whether he was present at any of these -- when any of these statements were taken, which I gave him in the binder, and I can proceed from that. Otherwise, I have no other way of knowing that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I apologise for this interruption, but we had to have this discussion. After you have reviewed the documents contained in the binder that I gave you, did you find in it any statement or Official Note for which you know in what way it was taken, or maybe you were present there; or did you do anything with relation to that note, or were you present at the time when the interviewee signed the statement?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment, I cannot remember being present while -- when this person signed this statement. I just went through the documents very quickly. I didn't have an opportunity to read them and familiarise myself with any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I ask one or two follow-up questions, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know a certain Edin Mrkalj?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise the family name. There was a Mrkalj who was a member of the public security station. Now whether that's one and the same person or whether it's this policeman or not ... anyway, I know the family name of Mrkalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I would just like to show one more document to this witness. This document has been translated, and depending on the witness's answer, I will decide whether I will tender this document into evidence. So can the witness please be shown 1D00-3623.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's tab 29 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is an Official Note dated the 2nd of June, 1992. On page 3 is the signature of an authorised official. I don't know if you can recognise the signature.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot be positive about whose signature this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is an Official Note relating to an interview conducted with Edin Mrkalj, and it says here that his profession was a police officer. Therefore, he was formerly employed with the SJB Prijedor, exactly the one that you mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know if this person, Edin Mrkalj, was at the Omarska investigation centre and if an interview was conducted with him?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm now whether he was at the Omarska investigation centre or not. All I know is there was a policeman by the name of Mrkalj.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, bearing in mind that the remaining questions that I intended to put to this witness refer mainly to this set of documents, and, as I understand the position of the Trial Chamber is as it is, then, in that case, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome. Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. Mr. Krgovic, it is -- as I indicated that we would have taken a break at 1.00, and it's just a minute or so before that, so we could -- we could take the 15-minute break and then we would resume, and then you would have a half-hour available to you before we rise for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it is a convenient time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] So we return in 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, while the witness is on his way in, we were alerted to the ten minutes that you needed to deal with some procedural matter, and what we are thinking is that the most efficient course would probably be to do that first thing tomorrow morning, and the witness who we probably aren't going to finish today could be instructed to return ten minutes into tomorrow morning's sitting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour. It was in relation to adjudicated facts negotiations, so that is all I wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dragan Krgovic. On behalf of Stojan Zupljanin Defence, I will be putting questions to you in relation to your testimony before the Tribunal. I will try and shorten my cross-examination of you today so that we would finish by the end of the day, but if you have any problems, please tell us so and we will make another break. The Prosecutor asked you how many criminal reports were submitted, or drafted by you, because you were not the ones who actually signed the reports; am I not correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. We weren't authorised to sign those. It was the duty of the senior officer of the organ. And in the initial stage, we prepared three criminal reports for -- against multiple individuals, charging them with armed rebellion and arming of population. I cannot remember what the third one was. It did involve Cirkin, Sead, but that was transferred to the army later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This last issue you discussed. I'd like to show you a document it's 2D103 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Mr. Krgovic repeat the number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, the interpreters would need you to repeat the number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2D03-1189.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you can find it under tab 35 in the Stanisic Defence binder. If you'd prefer it that way, I can hand over the document to you. It will be at the very end, number 35.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it. This report is in relation to Asim Muhic, also Kemal Alagic, and then there's another group of individuals mentioned below. Is there any need for me to read them out?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, there's no need. You told us that in relation to military investigation organs, that they dealt with the individuals that were somehow related to the army. You did mention the names of Alagic and Muhic as persons who were involved in the attack in commanding capacity. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kemal Alagic was a commander of one of the groups that took part on the attack on Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please take a look at the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the last page we see the signature. Is that what you're asking me about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it was signed by the Lieutenant-Colonel Radmilo Zeljaja, who was the commander of the Prijedor Brigade, 13th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, in addition to the preparations of reports that you drafted, there were also reports drafted by the military?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: They also used materials and notes from preliminary interviews you conducted about the attacks by Muslim and Croatian units against Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was part of the duties of our service. Namely, if there were any information that would fall under the jurisdiction of the army, we were duty-bound to submit them to the relevant military organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I -- we object because I don't think it is established that any of these perpetrators were at Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you would be so kind to look at the last page of this report, one can see listed there Official Notes that resulted from interviews with these individuals. And during his testimony, the witness told us about Kemal Alagic being in Omarska and that he knows of the case, if I haven't mistaken myself somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I don't believe that was the witness's testimony. If it is, I think that needs to be clarified. And with regard to the persons at the end of the document, with regard to the written statements, again, we don't know whether those individuals were at Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned Kemal Alagic during your testimony.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did mentioned Kemal Alagic. I mentioned him as the commander of the group that took part in the attacks against Prijedor. After the attack, he was at large for a while until he was arrested by the military in the area of Hambarine and the forest of Kurevo. So Alagic was not in Omarska, as far as I know at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Since these individuals were somehow linked up with the army, the entire documentation relevant for them was transferred to the military investigation organs, and they were in charge of it?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the usual practice. If the persons were under the military jurisdiction, we would submit documentation to them, and vice versa also applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm tendering this document for another reason. This document shows that in addition to the reports that had been submitted and drafted in Omarska, other reports had also been drafted. This shows that there was legal basis for detaining certain people.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But again, it does not apply to Omarska. This is a witness who is testifying about Omarska, and therefore he is not a witness that can say anything about this criminal report other than yes, he is aware that these persons were alleged to be leaders of groups that attempted to take over Prijedor on such and such a date. We are not getting further with the authenticity -- well, we don't challenge the authenticity of this document, but the relevance of this document has not been established, certainly not through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I confess, Mr. Krgovic, that I'm inclined, and I put no higher than that. At this point, I agree with Mr. Olmsted's objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before you continue, we could mark it for identification, pending introduction through another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is the only witness through whom we can introduce this one. I spoke about the work of the organs and how the whole job of interviewing and dividing people into three groups involved military organs as well. This particular criminal report was produced by military organs but there were also reported prepared by the civilian services involved in the procedure. This document is definitely relevant, because it speaks about the reasons and the ground for detention. The adjudicated facts about the categorisation of the detainees, and this the subject of the Prosecution's submission, and that is that people were detained at Omarska on the basis of their position in the Muslim community and on the basis of their standing, not on the basis of their taking part in an armed rebellion. This document, this criminal report, speaks completely contrary to that, and one should include the supporting material. That is something that both Mr. Zupljanin and Mr. Stanisic should have known about. If an inspector would come there to conduct auditing and to check why these people were detained, he would have looked at these reports and he would have realised that that constituted a basis for their detention. Therefore, all these documents contain the knowledge and the information that the accused in this trial could have had at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, again, could you clarify the relation between the witness and this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you please look at this document once again? And I do apologise. Page 2, tab 35.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at page 2? Not the last one; the one after the first page. In response to the question posed by Mr. Zecevic, you spoke about the groups that attacked Prijedor. You mentioned one of those groups led by -- look at paragraph 3 from the top. So the Slavko Ecimovic, Muhic, Asim, is leading a platoon that has one of the most delicate tasks to perform, which is an attack on the building of post office and police. And after that, other groups are mentioned, which is consistent with what you testified about. They took different routes of attack. And this is information that you had and this information is contained in this criminal report.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you submitted them to the military investigating organs as would be the case if the situation were reverse?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that I have established a sufficiently solid link between this document and this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would disagree with that. We don't think a link has been established at all. We have a criminal report. We don't have any indication that any of the perpetrators or manes listed in this report were detainees at Omarska. We have no indication that this witness had any involvement with the military prosecutor in drafting this criminal report. We have no idea what the outcome of this particular case is. The Defence is trying to tender this -- this criminal report to establish a particular event, an attack on Prijedor and who -- what happened on that particular day, and I don't believe this is reliable information to establish it, nor is this the appropriate witness to do it through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that witness ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, is this report written by the military police or by the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it was signed by the brigade military commander. And the witness confirmed that the basis for that was received from the organs who did the investigation at Omarska, because not only detainees were the subject of investigation at Omarska. They investigated the broader context. People who were not detained were also questioned, and later on, they were apprehended by the army. This is what we are trying to prove by refuting the adjudicated facts, and that is that Omarska was an investigation centre, not a centre intended to categorise people into groups to be executed or something like that. So through this line of questioning, we are seeking to refute the adjudicated fact for which this witness has been called. And this, relates to an armed rebellion. The major reason for the people being detained was an armed rebellion, and it should have been prosecuted by military organs since, at that time, the military organs were not operational, all of this was submitted to civilian organs and, later on, passed on to the military judicial which has already been confirmed by this witness today.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may make one more point. This criminal report is based upon three Official Notes that are listed at the end of this criminal report. We haven't established that any of those written statements were by interviewees or perpetrators who were at Omarska. So we do not have the link to the work that this witness did at Omarska and this criminal report that was filed by the military prosecutor, or by the military authorities with the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And if I may add that, Mr. Krgovic, it seems to me that even if, for the reasons that you have just stated, that this report may be admissible as relevant, I still don't see the nexus between it and the witness who is, at present, on the stand. That's the difficulty that -- that I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Plus, if I may add, the criminal report bears evidence of investigations done by the military authorities about a -- an armed rebellion or an armed attack that was carried out in Prijedor by members of Muslim and Croat forces, but that does not, in my view, undermine the facts that you are seeking to challenge. So the -- the purpose for which you seek to have this document introduced simply does not appear from the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will abide by the Chamber's ruling, and I will proceed with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let me put you a direct question. You said that you took part in the preparations of a number of criminal reports that were filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown 1D04-4308, tab --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Krgovic please repeat the number of the document and the number of the tab.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Look at 26 but I think it should be 27, in fact. And if you -- look at the page which has ERN 0041-5310.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise 1D04-3408.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Please move on. It's some dozen pages later. In the bottom, you will find the ERN 0041-5310.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It says: "Criminal report."

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the military court of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes -- no, no, I'm sorry. We should go further. You have gone too far, I think, in the binder. 415310 in the upper right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot find my bearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe you should better look at tab 26.

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Number 26 is the report -- oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The next one, please. Yes, that's the one, Muhamed Cehajic et al.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Just for the purposes of the record, it's page 29 in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You can see written on the top 4th of June?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This is a criminal report against Muhamed Cehajic, Mirza Mujajic and a number of other individuals. Is that one of the reports that you worked on?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is. I recall these names, Esef and Husein Crnkic, for example. And I think that these two were in Omarska. Muhamed Cehajic was in Omarska as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now you can see that, later on, this case was deferred to the military prosecutor's office and that they instituted proceedings; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-245 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can an exhibit number be given to this entire file? Or, rather, could it be first MFI'd, pending translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I suppose it should be marked for identification, pending translation. Which brings us to the end of today's sitting.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document be assigned Exhibit 2D00122 marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, unfortunately, your testimony is not yet at an end, so we will continue with -- tomorrow morning, and we expect to wrap up shortly after that. We would resume your testimony a little after the court itself resumes, so although we're going to take the adjournment to 9.00 in the morning, you wouldn't be escorted in until 9.10, or thereabouts. So if the usher would lower the blinds so that the witness could be escorted out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] I suppose we have to raise the blinds again to take the adjournment. Thank you. So we resume to tomorrow morning, and I believe we're still in this courtroom.
